disease_info: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by persistent, excessive worry about multiple domains of life that is difficult for the person to control and lasts for at least six months, often years. The anxiety is typically accompanied by physical and cognitive manifestations such as restlessness, fatigue, muscle tension, disturbed sleep, and difficulty concentrating, and it causes clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The course is usually chronic and fluctuating, with exacerbations during periods of increased stress and partial remissions rather than discrete episodes. It is distinguished from other anxiety disorders by its broad, non–situation-specific focus of worry (rather than circumscribed fears or panic attacks) and from mood disorders by the prominence of anxiety and tension rather than sustained low mood as the primary feature.

narrative.personality: He is a fiercely competitive, highly driven experimental physicist who is methodical, intellectually curious, and accustomed to pushing himself hard both in the lab and in demanding outdoor pursuits.
narrative.stressor: About fourteen months ago, Francisco’s lab secured a major multi-institution grant on sustainable energy materials, and he suddenly found himself leading a high-visibility project with aggressive milestones, complex collaborations, and the implicit expectation that he would convert it into top-tier publications and future funding. Initially he responded by doubling down on his characteristic intensity—taking on extra experiments, saying yes to every meeting, and treating long days and nights as a temporary sprint—but the constant grant deadlines, supervisory responsibilities, and competition with peer labs meant the pressure never actually eased. Over the following year, his work began to spill into every corner of his life: he stopped climbing and cycling regularly, postponed routine health checkups, and spent evenings mentally rehearsing experimental contingencies instead of unwinding, which gradually eroded his ability to recover between workdays and left him feeling depleted despite continuing to perform at a high level. He ultimately sought psychiatric help when his chronic overextension began to affect his reliability in the lab—he was making small but consequential planning errors, dreading going home because he couldn’t “switch off,” and noticed that his nights had become so disrupted that it was undermining both his productivity and enjoyment of the scientific work he usually loves.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m here because my sleep has been completely off for over a year, and it’s starting to mess with my work.”

narrative.personality: He is a methodical, detail-focused production veteran with a competitive streak who channels his energy into precision work, art, woodworking, and structured hobbies like home brewing and mindfulness practice.
narrative.stressor: Approximately a year and a few months ago, Kristian’s plant underwent a major restructuring with new automated lines, reduced staffing, and a shift in responsibilities that left him simultaneously training less-experienced coworkers and feeling implicitly responsible for keeping production targets on track. The new system came with frequent equipment glitches, pressure from management to minimize downtime, and a constant sense that any mistake could lead to safety incidents or job losses for his team, which tapped directly into his conscientiousness and long-standing tendency to mentally rehearse worst-case scenarios. Over time, this persistent performance pressure followed him home: he found it increasingly hard to enjoy his usual outlets like woodworking, basketball, and art outings because his mind kept looping back to possible production problems, potential layoffs, and whether he had overlooked something on his shift, which began to strain his patience with his family and reduce his engagement in activities that normally helped him decompress. He finally sought psychiatric care after realizing that his ability to focus on the line and during safety checks had noticeably declined, he was re-reading procedures without absorbing them, and both his supervisor and his spouse had commented that he seemed “constantly somewhere else” and more irritable, raising his own alarm that his mental state was now jeopardizing both work performance and home life.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to focus at work anymore—my mind keeps drifting and going blank, and it’s been getting worse over the past year.”

narrative.personality: She is a disciplined, achievement-driven construction manager with a meticulous, organized style who also has a reflective, artistic side that she usually nurtures through solitary creative and intellectual pursuits.
narrative.stressor: About fourteen months ago, Sheri and her spouse decided to start trying for a baby at the same time that she was assuming responsibility for a large, complex mixed-use project with ambitious sustainability targets and tight deadlines, creating parallel pressures in both her personal and professional lives. Early on, a minor medical scare related to fertility testing and a few tense conversations about timing and finances with her spouse left her feeling like every decision—taking on extra hours, saying yes to new responsibilities, even scheduling site visits—could have long-term consequences for their future family. Over the subsequent year, she increasingly carried these concerns with her everywhere: during BIM coordination meetings she found herself preoccupied with whether she was neglecting her marriage, at home she was mentally running project schedules and code compliance risks, and her usual calming activities like painting, journaling, and gardening turned into spaces where she mulled over every possible outcome rather than truly relaxing, gradually eroding her sense of control and emotional resilience. She eventually sought psychiatric help when she noticed that her preoccupation with “what if” scenarios was consuming most of her mental bandwidth—she was less present with her spouse, had difficulty enjoying art or reading without her thoughts spiraling back to work and family decisions, and felt that she could no longer rein in the constant stream of worries on her own.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like my mind is always racing with worries, and I can’t seem to shut it off anymore.”
